clue.text: Sort of holiday some rugby players must have time for

blocks.note: the pack is the eight forwards — only some of a rugby side
an age = a long time

explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' is the fair-play word: a pack is part of a rugby side, never the whole fifteen. The surface, players hoping for a break, keeps both halves sounding like sport.
explanation.definitionFit: A package holiday bundles flights, hotel and transfers into one purchase, so the word names that sort of holiday by the deal it arrives as.

clue.text: Maintains focus for cryptic clues

indicators.note: a focus is the central point of something, so the word it governs yields only the letter at its centre

blocks.note: seven letters, and the fourth — the middle one — is P
clues = leads, the things a detective follows up

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is describing what you are looking at, which is the joke, and both halves of the wordplay come out of those same two words rather than from anywhere else in the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: To plead innocence is to maintain it: both verbs mean asserting something and sticking to it, in court or out of it.

clue.text: Without using tons, strangely it does not enhance crisp flavour

indicators.note: to go without something is to do the job in its absence
a thing done strangely comes out other than it went in, and letters are no exception

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for a ton, so 'tons' is two of them — and both are left out
the same words once both Ts have gone: fourteen letters to rearrange

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pretends to be sceptical about something that is plainly true of crisps. Bank the abbreviation: one ton is T, so a plural asks for the letter twice.
explanation.definitionFit: It is one of the two or three flavours every crisp aisle carries, so the definition names the answer by example rather than by meaning.

clue.text: David Beckham makes one eat dessert first

indicators.note: 'first' fixes where a piece goes rather than what it is — the pudding is served at the front of the build, not at the end of the meal

blocks.note: afters = pudding, the course that comes after the main
to have lunch is to eat it

explanation.walkthrough: Beckham's name has been on a range of men's fragrances for years, so the opening words are the definition and not a joke about football.
explanation.definitionFit: He licenses his name to men's grooming products, so the 'one' he makes is a scent — a definition by the celebrity product rather than by the word.

clue.text: Silver lining – occasionally he’ll get two below par

indicators.note: a lining sits inside the thing it lines
what happens occasionally happens every now and then instead of all the way through, so only every other letter is taken

blocks.note: every second letter of hE'lL gEt
AG is the chemical symbol for silver, from argentum

explanation.walkthrough: 'Silver lining' is an idiom pulled in two: the silver is a chemical symbol and the lining is an instruction, and neither has anything to do with clouds.
explanation.definitionFit: In golf a hole played two strokes under par is an eagle — the bird names the score, one better than a birdie.

clue.text: Cup of tea turned up with a little Bounty Bar?

indicators.note: something turned faces the other way, so those two letters arrive in the opposite order
a little of a word is the smallest piece you can take of it — the letter it starts with

blocks.note: a brew is a cup of tea
UP, turned round
just a little of Bounty — its opening letter

explanation.walkthrough: The trick is where you split 'Bounty Bar': the surface glues them into a chocolate bar, while the clue wants the Bounty for one letter and the Bar for the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A brewpub is a pub that brews its own beer on the premises, and a pub is a bar — the question mark covers the narrowing.

clue.text: Supply gum rubber – wanting metre on new roll?

indicators.note: read as the adverb from supple — done in a bendy way
to be wanting something is to lack it

blocks.note: GUM RUBBER once the M has gone
m = metre — the letter that is missing
n = new, joining the letters to be shuffled

explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' is the whole joke: it reads as a verb about providing things and is really the adverb from supple. A word that changes its stress is a setter's favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: A burger bun is a soft round roll, so 'roll' names it by category — the question mark admitting it is only one kind.

clue.text: 2 seconds to read advertising watchdog’s email

indicators.note: a second is the one after the first, so each word here gives up whatever letter is standing in position two

blocks.note: rEad — second letter
aDvertising — second letter
wAtchdog's — second letter
eMail — second letter

explanation.walkthrough: '2 seconds' reads as no time at all and is really two jobs in two words: the number points across at another answer, and the plural picks the letters. The watchdog is a decoy.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition is the cross-reference: 2 down is CHEESE, and this is the round red Dutch one, so it belongs to that class.

clue.text: Walkman – perhaps as Spooner relates playing …

indicators.note: play is loose movement — the give in a rope or a rudder — so letters with play in them will not stay where they were put

blocks.note: fourteen letters, exactly the fourteen wanted, in another order

explanation.walkthrough: Naming Spooner sends you hunting for swapped opening sounds. Here the reverend is not an instruction at all — his name is raw material, and 'playing' is the only order given.
explanation.definitionFit: Walkman was Sony's brand of the thing, so the definition names the answer by its most famous example, which is what 'perhaps' admits.

clue.text: … one from The Strokes (unoriginal pop group, according to him)

indicators.note: 'him' is the Reverend Spooner, named in the clue above, and quoting him means the opening sounds of two words trade places

blocks.note: hack = derivative, churned out to a formula
a band is a pop group
say HACK BAND with the opening sounds swapped, H for B, and you get the answer

explanation.walkthrough: The Strokes are a real band, so the surface has a pop group where the answer has tennis. A spoonerism always announces itself: someone in the clue is doing the talking.
explanation.definitionFit: A backhand is one of the strokes in tennis, so the phrase names it by example while the capitals point at the group instead.

clue.text: Possibility of outlet store finally opening

indicators.note: what comes finally comes last, so the shop hands over only its closing letter
an opening is the way in, so that letter is placed at the front rather than anywhere else

blocks.note: the last letter of storE
a vent is an outlet for air

explanation.walkthrough: 'Outlet', 'store' and 'opening' are all retail words in the surface and not one of them is a shop in the wordplay — the outlet is an air vent and the opening is a position.
explanation.definitionFit: 'In the event of rain' means 'if rain happens', and that is the sense wanted here: something that may occur.

clue.text: I worked with cash register she’s discarded – it’s old

indicators.note: dough is worked — pushed about until it takes a different shape, which is what happens to these letters
to discard is to throw away, so those four letters are gone before any shuffling starts

blocks.note: the setter's own I, one letter of the mixture
twelve letters with four thrown away
S, H, E and S — the four letters discarded from CASH REGISTER

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a small shop being cleared out. A long anagram with a deletion inside it is best checked by counting: twelve letters, minus four, plus one makes nine.
explanation.definitionFit: Geriatric is the medical adjective for aged, used loosely of anything long past its best, so it stands for the plain word.

clue.text: Confused as senior coppers demanded …

blocks.note: a DI is a detective inspector; more than one of them gives DIs
to order something is to demand it

explanation.walkthrough: Police ranks are worth banking — DI for inspector, DS for sergeant, PC for constable — and pluralising an abbreviation with S is standard, which is what hides the join here.
explanation.definitionFit: Something disordered has been thrown out of its order, and a mind in that state is confused — one word covers a messy room and a muddled head.

clue.text: … commanding officer essentially use the truncheon

indicators.note: the essence of a word is what sits at its heart, and here it governs two little words at once, each giving up its centre

blocks.note: CO is the standard abbreviation for a commanding officer
the middle letters of uSe and tHe

explanation.walkthrough: One indicator governing two words at once is what makes this hard to see, and the ellipsis helps it hide: the words read as an order being passed down from the clue before.
explanation.definitionFit: A cosh is a short heavy stick carried as a weapon, which is exactly what a policeman's truncheon is — the two name one object.

clue.text: Allowed to take caravan briefly – that is assuming posh car up front is connected? Not so

indicators.note: taking something is holding it, so one piece ends up inside the other instead of alongside it
to assume something is to take it on board, so the pair is taken in rather than added at the end
up front is at the near end, so the insertion happens at the start of the piece and not deep inside it

blocks.note: i.e. = that is
RR is Rolls-Royce, the byword for a posh car, taken in at the front
let = allowed, as a flat is let
a caravan is a van for short, and it goes inside

explanation.walkthrough: Two insertions in one clue and both hide inside ordinary verbs, 'take' and 'assuming'. The surface — a caravan towed behind a Rolls-Royce — is pure decoy.
explanation.definitionFit: Relevant means connected to the matter in hand, and 'Not so' turns it round, which is the job the IR- prefix does to the word.

clue.text: Firm steal something many people like to drive

definitions.text: something many people like to drive

blocks.note: firm = hard, unyielding
a steal is a bargain — something bought far too cheaply

explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive' is the giveaway once you stop picturing cars. Both halves are everyday synonyms, which is why the surface glides past without sounding like wordplay at all.
explanation.definitionFit: To drive a hard bargain is to negotiate ruthlessly — the definition works on the whole idiom, not on either word by itself.

clue.text: Can rule Tottenham’s first 11 out – ultimately not up for it

indicators.note: the number sends you to another clue in this grid, and that answer is a word for jumbled — the instruction is borrowed from it
ultimately means at the very end, so only the closing letter of the word before it is taken

blocks.note: three letters of the mixture, straight off the clue
four more, again just as written
the opening letter of Tottenham
the last letter of ouT

explanation.walkthrough: The football surface is the decoy: no first team, no eleven players, just letters. Using a cross-reference as the instruction is the neat touch — a number standing in for the word it answers.
explanation.definitionFit: If you are not up for something you are unwilling to do it, so the everyday phrase is doing duty as the adjective.

clue.text: Made cloudy as former students smoked

blocks.note: an OB is an old boy, a former pupil; more than one gives OBs
smoking meat or fish is one way of curing it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Smoked' does quiet work: curing covers salting and drying as well, so the clue offers one example of the wider word. OB for old boy is standard crossword shorthand.
explanation.definitionFit: To obscure something is to dim or blur it, so glass or a sky that has been made cloudy has been obscured — same tense, same sense.

clue.text: See 2
Goodness – neighbour’s entrance buzzer rings with excessive force – I must hide

indicators.note: to ring something is to encircle it
what hides goes out of sight, so that letter is not there when the word is written out

blocks.note: a bee is the buzzer, and it opens up to take a letter in
the first letter of Neighbour
VIOLENCE is force past what is needed, with one letter no longer visible
the letter that must hide, taken out of VIOLENCE

explanation.walkthrough: A doorbell going in the surface, an insect in the wordplay. The long word arrives almost whole, so the work is spotting that four of its letters were built separately first.
explanation.definitionFit: Benevolence is the disposition to wish others well, and goodness in the sense of kindness rather than virtue is exactly that.

clue.text: See 7
Teasing related to exploit

blocks.note: to play with someone is to tease them, and play is jest — 'said in play'
on = about: a book on birds is a book related to birds

explanation.walkthrough: Three words, each of which could be the definition, which is what makes the split hard to find. ON for 'about' is a workhorse — two letters out of a preposition.
explanation.definitionFit: To play on someone's fears is to exploit them: the phrasal verb means working a weakness for your own ends.

clue.text: Show off contribution to murder

blocks.note: to boast loudly about a win, the way a rooster sounds off at dawn
a murder is the collective noun for these birds, so one of them helps make one up

explanation.walkthrough: 'Murder' is the trap — a crime in the surface, a collective noun in the definition. The bird's is the best known of all of them, which is what makes the joke land.
explanation.definitionFit: Crowing is boasting loudly over a triumph, and a murder is the collective noun for the birds, so a single one is a contribution to it.

clue.text: A Western losing Oscar – that’s unexpected

indicators.note: what is lost is no longer there, so the word that follows gives up the letter it is losing

blocks.note: the clue's own A, opening the build
OCCIDENTAL means western, and its first letter has gone
Oscar is O in the NATO alphabet — that is the letter lost

explanation.walkthrough: A perfect sentence about the film awards, and none of it is about films. Occidental for western and Oscar for O are both worth banking for next time.
explanation.definitionFit: Something accidental happens by chance rather than by design, which is precisely what nobody sees coming — the everyday sense of the word.

clue.text: One wood is perfect

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
deal is fir or pine timber, sold as sawn planks

explanation.walkthrough: Deal is the piece to learn: it looks like a bargain or a hand of cards, and in crosswords it is very often the softwood instead.
explanation.definitionFit: An ideal solution is a perfect one — the adjective sense, meaning nothing about it could be improved.

clue.text: Perhaps Rosemary is writing her book

blocks.note: taken straight from the clue
b = book, the standard abbreviation

explanation.walkthrough: Rosemary is a woman in the surface and a plant in the definition, and the capital letter costs the setter nothing — every clue begins with one.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosemary is one of the kitchen herbs, so the definition works by example, and 'Perhaps' is the flag that says as much.

clue.text: It must go through on time they regularly stress

indicators.note: going through something means passing inside it, so this piece is planted in the middle of the rest
taken regularly means at an even step through the word — every other letter, not the lot

blocks.note: re = on, as in a memo headed 're: your letter'
straight from the clue, and it goes inside the rest
an era is a stretch of time
every other letter of They — T and E

explanation.walkthrough: Three tiny words each hand over a standard crossword piece, RE, ERA and a pair of alternate letters, while the surface talks about a deadline and gives nothing away.
explanation.definitionFit: To reiterate a point is to say it again for emphasis, and to stress a point is the same act of insisting on it.

clue.text: Order Andrew’s source to meet King Charles, say

indicators.note: a river's source is where it starts, so the name gives up the letter it begins with
two pieces that meet stand side by side, so they are simply written one after the other
'say' means 'for example'

blocks.note: the letter Andrew starts from
R for Rex, Latin for king — the R that follows a monarch's name
the famous Charles is Ray Charles, so the example hands over his first name

explanation.walkthrough: Three royal names in a row is deliberate, and only the middle one is royalty in the wordplay. The soul singer is hiding behind a prince and a king.
explanation.definitionFit: An array is things set out in ranks and rows, the sense preserved in 'in battle array' — order as an arrangement rather than as a command.

clue.text: Fool taking smack maybe loves to escape

indicators.note: 'maybe' says the word is only an instance
what escapes gets out, so those letters leave the words they were sitting in

blocks.note: DOING = taking, the way you do or take drugs, with one letter escaped
a smack is a small fishing BOAT, again one letter lighter
love is nothing, the O of tennis scoring; two loves are two Os, and both get out

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is entirely about drugs and the answer is entirely about a fool. A smack being a fishing boat is the fact that unlocks it; love for O is standard.
explanation.definitionFit: A dingbat is American slang for a scatterbrained idiot, so the definition is a plain synonym — a noun standing in for a noun.

clue.text: Drunk dwelt on disappointment

indicators.note: a drunk cannot walk a straight line, and letters in that state will not stay in the order they were given

blocks.note: seven letters, the seven the answer needs, in a different order

explanation.walkthrough: Dwelling on something is exactly what people do with a disappointment, which is why the surface holds together — and the fodder sits in plain sight as the sentence's verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A let-down is the flat feeling left when something promised fails to arrive, so it is a plain noun synonym.
